POSITION SPECIFICS The Department of Kinesiology and the Department of Mechanical Engineering, in partnership with the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences, invite applications for a tenure-line faculty position at the rank of Associate or Full Professor in Biomechanics and Biorobotics . The successful candidate will also serve as the Director of the Center for Movement Science and Technology (C-MOST) within the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences. The anticipated start date is Fall 2027. This is a strategic leadership opportunity for an internationally recognized scholar to help shape the future of biomechanics and biorobotics at Penn State. The successful candidate will lead the continued development of C-MOST while establishing a broader interdisciplinary Biorobotics Research Cluster that connects and facilitates world-class research across Penn State's colleges, institutes, and campuses. The Opportunity Penn State has longstanding strengths in biomechanics, movement science, engineering, the life sciences, neuroscience, materials, computation, medicine, and human health. C-MOST provides a foundation for bringing these complementary strengths together around fundamental questions of movement and the development of transformative technologies. We seek an accomplished scientist, engineer, or physician-scientist with an outstanding record of scholarly achievement, external research funding, interdisciplinary collaboration, and scientific leadership. The successful candidate will develop and advance a compelling vision for C-MOST and create new opportunities for collaboration among researchers, engineers, clinicians, and external partners. The Director will be expected to build C-MOST as a platform for interdisciplinary discovery and technology development while advancing a broader vision for Biorobotics at Penn State . This effort will bring together expertise spanning biomechanics and neuromechanics, robotics and control, biological systems, materials, computation, medicine, rehabilitation, and human performance. The position provides an opportunity for a senior scholar to help define a field at the intersection of biology, movement, engineering, and robotics and to build research programs that extend from fundamental discovery to technologies with meaningful applications in health, medicine, performance, and beyond. The Director will also contribute to the strategic activities and administration of C-MOST, including personnel, budgetary resources, research infrastructure, development activities, education and outreach, and engagement with internal and external partners. Importantly, this is a faculty leadership position . The successful candidate will maintain an independent, externally funded research program and will contribute to undergraduate and graduate education and mentorship. Areas of Research We seek candidates whose scholarship contributes to the broad and rapidly evolving field of biomechanics and biorobotics. Areas of interest include, but are not limited to: Human and biological movement biomechanics Neuromechanics and sensorimotor control Biorobotics and bio-inspired robotics Human-robot interaction Assistive and rehabilitative robotics Wear

The position is ideal for candidates interested in pursuing PhD studies in Economics, particularly those with an interest in psychologically-grounded economic theory. Fellows will aid Professor Rabin and others in formally drawing out the implications of theoretical models in both “behavioral” and “classical” economic theory. Particular emphasis will be put in psychologically-grounded models that attempt to rigorously improve the psychological realism of economic theory. Examples of such improvements include incorporating limited rationality (e.g., errors in statistical reasoning, errors in interpreting others’ behavior), time-inconsistent preferences (self-control problems, utility misprediction), and more general utility functions (e.g., dependent on expectations, self-image, and other beliefs) into our models.* This research agenda maintains the conventional mathematical tools and formalism of economic theory, and is outlined in Rabin’s 2013 AER and JEL papers. The goal is to develop and evaluate models that can broadly improve economics, rather than over-stating the successes or failures of theories by cherry picking examples, or ignoring the cases where the new theories make worse predictions than classical economics or competing new general formulations. The research assistance needed will reflect this goal: participants will be asked to rigorously work out both realistic and unrealistic implications of models in areas such as game theory, choice under uncertainty, belief updating, social learning, etc. Per the list of key responsibilities and qualifications below, please pay attention to the nature of this position. There are a great many pre-doctoral positions geared towards lab experiments, field experiments, and other empirical methods, with fantastic PI’s, and naturally fitting in the category of “behavioral economics”, where you will be able to leverage and build skills in such research. This is not such a position. Develop tools to streamline the application of these models. • Assist with specific research papers on psychologically-grounded economic theory. • Conduct literature reviews on theory and evidence broadly related to behavioral economics. • Analyze and evaluate what existing empirical and experimental evidence tells us about different behavioral theories. job_a83fce4e2bd8ea24: About the Opportunity Job Summary Northeastern University’s Coastal Sustainability Institute (CSI) and The Nature Conservancy’s (TNC) Massachusetts and Global Science programs are partnering to offer a joint Postdoctoral Fellowship Opportunity in Coastal Sustainability. ​ ​ Northeastern University (NU) is a global leader in experiential education and research with expertise in marine and coastal ecology, environmental forecasting and climate adaptation, fisheries and ecosystem-based management, ecological engineering and restoration, environmental sociology, and sustainability science. ​ The Nature Conservancy is a world-leading conservation organization with marine priorities currently focused on sustainable fisheries, quantifying the economic benefits of coastal conservation, and the role of ecosystems in protecting societies from coastal hazards and climate change. ​ ​ NU and TNC are active partners in coastal conservation and sustainability science research and practice. As part of this ongoing partnership, NU’s CSI and TNC are excited to announce the fourth round of this Coastal Sustainability Fellows Program for postdoctoral scientists. ​ ​ The CSI-TNC Coastal Sustainability Fellows Program will foster a collaborative, intellectual environment that leverages the interdisciplinary expertise of both CSI and TNC to train postdoctoral scholars and address major challenges facing coastal communities and ecosystems. Qualifications The CSI- TNC Coastal Sustainability Fellows Program welcomes applicants from all fields of study focused on understanding and implementing solutions that promote coastal sustainability. Applicants must have earned a doctoral degree in a relevant field of natural science, social science, or engineering. The 2026 Fellowship competition will prioritize applicants with research interests related to coastal restoration, marsh migration, and community adaptation to flood risk. While not exclusive, specific areas of research connected to these priorities could include: • Addressing ecological and social barriers and enabling factors for coastal restoration, including salt marshes, oysters, and seagrasses • Understanding factors that influence land use decisions related to coastal flood risk, including floodplain protection, coastal relocation, restoration potential, and local socio-ecological dynamics • Identifying and facilitating marsh migration corridors Fellowship Details & Application Process Based on funding availability, the fellowship will provide two years of salary ($60,315 per year) and benefits plus an additional $5,000 each year to support travel for meetings and field research. Fellows will be based at NU’s CSI and Marine Science Center in Nahant, MA, and co-mentored by scientists at CSI and TNC. In addition to research, fellows will have opportunities to develop skills consistent with their goals including grant writing / fundraising, teaching, mentoring, and networking with TNC and academic partners. Initial review of applications will begin on September 21, with an anticipated start date as early as October 2026. Complete applications will include a CV, 2-4 representative publications, names and contact information for 2-3 individuals who can provide letters of recommendation, a 1-page broader impacts statement, and a 2-page research statement that identifies an academic mentor (or mentors) at CSI, and how their research will also link to TNC mentors in the Massachusetts Ocean and Climate programs. Prospective candidates should contact Alison Bowden at TNC and their potential academic mentor at CSI before applying. We are committed to promoting diversity in conservation and sustainability science and therefore strongly encourage applicants from all historically marginalized groups. The duration of this position is contingent upon the continued availability of funding from this award at its current financial level. For questions about the fellowship, please contact: Randall Hughes at rhughes

The Research Fellow in Domestic Labor History is a fixed-term, 30-hour per week position. The expected salary range for this job opportunity is: $42.74 to $47.01 per hour. The Research Fellow in Domestic Labor History will conduct original primary-source research to provide evidence for the Museum to document and interpret the domestic conditions that afforded Emily Dickinson the opportunity to compose a large body of poetic and epistolary work. Working with archival, manuscript, and material culture collections, the Fellow will examine records including correspondence, financial documents, census data, maps, employment records, newspapers, church records, artifacts, landscapes, the built environment, and other contemporaneous sources to identify and reconstruct the lives and labor of individual domestic workers associated with Dickinson family households and comparable homes in the region. The Fellow will investigate and analyze the social, economic, and cultural structures of nineteenth-century Amherst and New England—including systems of race, gender, class, ethnicity, immigration, and labor—that shaped the experiences, opportunities, and constraints of domestic workers. This work will situate individual biographies within broader regional contexts of domestic service, wage labor, household economies, and shifting social hierarchies. The Fellow will assess how visible and invisible labor within the home—including cooking, cleaning, laundry, caregiving, agricultural labor, animal husbandry, and other forms of household and homestead management—contributed to sustaining social, psychic, and material environments in which employers could pursue intellectual, professional, civic, and creative endeavors. The position requires critical attention to gaps and silences in the historical record and interpretive possibilities for representing individuals whose lives were often minimally documented. The Fellow will produce well-documented research findings and will work with the Senior Director of Programs to develop an interpretive framework from these findings. The Museum may incorporate research results into the visitor experience through interpretation, public programs, exhibitions, publications, and institutional scholarship, thereby advancing a fuller and more inclusive account of the historical conditions that supported Dickinson’s authorship. job_e494a15351cdccfe: Job Description Summary Organization's Summary Statement: Human beings share a capacity for language, unique to the species. This capacity guides the learning of language in children and constrains the character of the languages we come to have. To study it we pursue various sources of evidence. Among them are the grammars of individual languages; patterns of grammatical variation across languages; the development, normal and abnormal, of language in children; the mental processing of language in use; and the embodiment of language in the brain. But all these perspectives converge on a single natural object: the human language faculty, whose study unifies the work at Maryland Linguistics. The Department of Linguistics at the University of Maryland combines current theoretical research in phonology, syntax, and semantics with state-of-the-art experimental research in language acquisition, computational linguistics, psycholinguistics and neurolinguistics, in order to understand the human capacity for language. Connections between our core competencies are strong, with theoretical, experimental and computational work typically pursued in tandem. A network of collaboration at all levels sustains a research climate that is both vigorous and friendly. Here new ideas develop in conversation, stimulated by the steady activity of our labs and research groups, frequent student meetings with faculty, regular talks by local and invited scholars and collaborations with a campus community of over 200 language scientists.
